title: How the Electric Fan Saved Cities Before AC Conquered the South
fullText: In the summer of 1896, a wave of heat settled over the eastern United States and refused to leave. For 10 straight days, temperatures across New York City climbed past 100°. The air in lower Manhattan became so thick and still that people in tenement buildings on the Lower East Side dragged their mattresses onto fire escapes and rooftops just to breathe. Horses pulling street cars collapsed on the cobblestone roads of Broadway and were left where they fell because the city couldn't collect the carcasses fast enough. City morgs in Manhattan and Brooklyn ran out of space within 72 hours. The New York City coroner's office recorded over 1,300 heat deaths in under 2 weeks. And New York wasn't even the worst of it. In Chicago, workers at the Union stockyards on the south side dropped where they stood. Entire city blocks in the tenement districts went quiet because families had no way to cool down. No running water in many buildings and no escape from apartments that had turned into ovens. Across the eastern seabboard, the final count was staggering. Over 1,500 people dead in a single heatwave. What nobody knew at the time was that a small humming machine already sitting on desks in a handful of wealthy offices held the answer. Not air conditioning. That was still decades away. Something far simpler. A set of spinning blades powered by an electric motor. The electric fan. But this story doesn't start with the fan itself. It starts with the heat. Because to understand why one simple machine mattered so much, you have to understand what heat was actually doing to American cities, especially in the South, long before anyone figured out how to fight it. Think about what cities looked like in the 1880s and 1890s. Up north, places like New York, Boston, and Philadelphia were booming. Factories, immigration, railroads, all of it concentrated in the Northeast and the Great Lakes region. Population growth in those cities was explosive. But head south below the Mason Dixon line, and the picture looked completely different. Cities like Houston, Atlanta, New Orleans, and Dallas existed, sure, but they were small, much smaller than you'd expect. Houston in 1880 had a population of roughly 16,000 people. Atlanta had around 37,000. Compare that to Chicago, which had already blown past 500,000 and was racing toward a million. The gap was enormous. And it wasn't just about industry or railroads or immigration patterns. It was the heat. Southern summers were a wall. June through September in Houston, temperatures regularly sat above 95° with humidity so thick it felt like wearing a wet blanket. In New Orleans, the combination of Mississippi River swamp air and relentless sun created conditions that were borderline dangerous just to walk around in. Atlanta's red clay hills baked under a sun that didn't let up from May to October. And this wasn't just uncomfortable, it was a genuine obstacle to growth. Factories couldn't run efficiently when workers were passing out on the floor. Offices couldn't stay open in the afternoon because the indoor temperature in a brick building in downtown Houston would climb past 105° by 2 in the afternoon. Merchants closed their shops. Courts shortened their sessions. State legislatures in places like Austin and Baton Rouge would adjourn for the entire summer because the capital buildings became physically unbearable. I mean, think about that for a second. Entire governments shutting down because the building was too hot. So, people adapted and the ways they adapted shaped everything about how the South looked and felt. Architecture was the most obvious response. The shotgun house, that long, narrow style you still see across New Orleans and Memphis, wasn't a design choice. It was a survival strategy. Every room lined up front to back with doors at each end so a breeze could pass straight through the entire house like a tunnel. The dog trot cabin, popular across rural Alabama, Mississippi, and Georgia, was built as two separate rooms connected by a covered open air breezeway in the middle. That breezeway was the coolest spot on the property and families basically lived in it from June to September. Sleeping porches became standard on middle-class homes across the south. These were screened in upper level porches where the whole family would drag their beds on summer nights because the indoor bedrooms were unbearable after absorbing a full day of sun. In cities like Savannah and Charleston, the piaza, a long side porch running the full length of the house, became the defining architectural feature. The entire house was oriented to catch whatever breeze might drift in off the coast. Even city planning reflected the problem. Streets in older southern cities were often wider than their northern counterparts because wider streets meant better air circulation between buildings. Public squares and parks weren't just aesthetic choices. They were ventilation strategy. Trees weren't decorative. They were infrastructure. And daily life bent around the heat, too. Work in agricultural communities started before dawn and stopped by midday. In cities, offices and shops ran on a split schedule. Open in the morning, closed through the worst afternoon hours, then sometimes reopening in the evening. Social life happened after dark on porches, in town squares, at outdoor gatherings where the temperature had finally dropped below 90. The whole rhythm of southern life was built around one simple brutal fact. The heat was in charge and humans just had to work around it. But there was a cost to all this adaptation. Southern cities couldn't grow the way northern ones could. You couldn't build a dense vertical downtown when every building became an oven in summer. You couldn't attract northern investment when half the workforce was unreliable from June to September because of heat illness. You couldn't convince immigrants who were flooding into New York and Chicago by the millions to settle in a place where the climate itself felt hostile. The South was stuck. Beautiful, culturally rich, deeply rooted, but stuck. Its cities couldn't compete with the industrial north because the weather wouldn't let them. And nobody had a real solution. You could build your house to catch a breeze. You could adjust your schedule. You could sit on your porch with a hand fan and a glass of sweet tea and wait for October, but you couldn't change the air. For a while, things actually seemed like they would just stay that way forever. The South would remain agricultural, slower paced, and defined by the limitations of its climate. Northern newspapers even wrote about it in exactly those terms, treating the southern heat as a kind of permanent condition that explained everything about the region's economy and temperament. It was just how things were. That didn't last because in 1882, in a small workshop connected to the Crocker and Curtis Electric Motor Company in New York City, a 22-year-old engineer named Skyler Scott's Wheeler was about to change everything. and the machine he built could fit on a desk. Skyler Scott's Wheeler wasn't trying to save cities. He was just trying to solve a problem with a motor. Wheeler was a young engineer working at the Crocker and Curtis Electric Motor Company, a small outfit operating out of a workshop in lower Manhattan. The company made electric motors for industrial use, the kind that powered printing presses and factory equipment. Wheeler spent his days tinkering with ways to make these motors smaller, lighter, and more practical. And at some point in 1882, he attached two spinning blades directly to a small electric motor, set it on a desk, and turned it on. That was it. The thing had no housing, no cage around the blades, and no oscillation. Just a bare motor with two exposed blades whipping through the air on a tabletop. It looked almost dangerous, and honestly, it kind of was, but it moved air. And in a stuffy Manhattan office in the middle of August, that mattered more than safety. Wheeler called it a desk fan. The Crocker and Curtis Company sold a handful of them to businesses in the city, mostly banks and law offices, where the partners could afford the novelty, because that's exactly what the electric fan was in 1882, a novelty. These early units cost around $40 at a time when the average American worker earned roughly $400 a year. Adjusted for today, that's the equivalent of spending somewhere north of $350 on a single fan. That's the kind of number that makes accountants cry. So, the electric fan entered the world as a rich man's toy. A curiosity sitting on the mahogany desk of a bank president in downtown Manhattan while the rest of the city sweltered in 100 degree tenementss five blocks away. If the story had ended there, nobody would remember Skylar Wheeler's name. But other engineers noticed what he built. And they saw something Wheeler himself might not have fully appreciated. They saw scale. The 1890s were a golden era for American manufacturing. and the electric fan landed right in the middle of it. Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Power Station had already begun electrifying parts of lower Manhattan in 1882. The same year Wheeler built his prototype, alternating current systems from Westinghouse and George Westinghouse's partnership with Nicola Tesla was spreading electrical grids to cities across the country through the 1890s. For the first time, there was an infrastructure to plug things into and fan makers pounced. Emerson Electric, founded in Saint Louie in 1890 became one of the first companies to mass-produce electric fans for home and office use. Their early models were bulky, heavy iron contraptions with brass blades, but they worked. General Electric followed quickly, leveraging the enormous manufacturing base they built under Edison and his successors. Westinghouse jumped in too, using their alternating current motor technology to build fans that could run on the newer AC power grids spreading across the Midwest and South. The competition between these three companies drove innovation at a speed that feels almost modern. In 1894, Emerson introduced the first oscillating fan, a motor that rotated the entire fan head back and forth so it could cool a wider area instead of just blasting air in one direction. It sounds simple now, but at the time, this was a genuine breakthrough. A single fan could now cool an entire office or parlor instead of just the person sitting directly in front of it. Then came the blade guard. Early fans like Wheeler's original had completely exposed spinning blades. You'd set one on your desk and hope nobody leaned in too close. General Electric started adding wire cages around the blades in the late 1890s, which opened up a completely new market. Suddenly, you could put an electric fan in a home with children. You could put one in a school room. You could put one in a hospital ward without worrying about a patient losing a finger. The blade guard didn't make the fan work better. It made the fan possible for everyone. And the prices kept falling. That's the part that actually changed history. In 1895, a decent electric fan still cost between $25 and $40. By 1905, increased competition and improved manufacturing had pushed prices down to around $15. By 1912, Emerson was advertising fans for under $10. And by the early 1920s, a workingclass family in Birmingham, Alabama or Memphis, Tennessee, could walk into a hardware store and pick up a reliable oscillating electric fan for $5 or $6. That was real money, sure, but it was reachable. A family could save up for a couple of weeks and buy one. This decision seemed small at the time. It wasn't because what happened over the next two decades is one of those stories that never made the history books but reshaped the entire country. The electric fan went from a luxury item in a Manhattan bank office to a mass market appliance sitting in kitchens, bedrooms, factory floors, and storefronts from Virginia to Texas. Production numbers tell the story. In 1900, American companies produced roughly 500,000 electric fans. By 1910, that number had climbed past 2 million. By 1920, annual production was somewhere around 4 1/2 million units. Fans were pouring into American homes faster than almost any other appliance, except the light bulb. And here's the detail that everyone missed at the time. The fans weren't selling evenly across the country. They were selling disproportionately in the south. The region that needed them the most was buying them the fastest. The same cities that had been stuck for decades, held back by brutal summers and an inability to keep workers productive or buildings habitable past June, were suddenly placing orders by the train load. Hardware stores in Houston, Atlanta, New Orleans, Dallas, and Jacksonville couldn't keep fans in stock during spring buying season. Sears Robuck Catalogs, which reached rural communities across the Deep South, featured electric fans prominently starting in the early 1900s. For the first time, a family in rural Mississippi, or a shopkeeper in Galveastston, Texas, had a way to fight back against the heat that didn't involve rearranging their entire life around it. The same thing that built the electric fan success, its simplicity, and its price was about to become the thing that rebuilt the American South. But that's getting ahead of the story. Because before the fan could transform a region, it had to transform something smaller first. It had to transform a single room, a single factory floor, a single department store on a Tuesday afternoon in July. And what happened inside those rooms would change the way Americans thought about where they could live, where they could work, and what kind of city was actually possible in a place where the thermometer regularly hit triple digits. Picture a textile mill in Charlotte, North Carolina around 1910. It's July. The building is brick, two stories, no insulation, and packed with 150 workers operating looms and spindles that generate their own heat on top of whatever the sun is already doing outside. Before electric fans, factories like this one ran on a skeleton crew from June through September. Workers couldn't last a full shift. Foreman would rotate people off the floor every couple of hours because the indoor temperature would climb past 110° by midday. Production dropped by as much as 40% during peak summer. The heat wasn't just uncomfortable, it was costing factory owners real money. Then someone bolted a row of 20in oscillating fans to the ceiling beams. The effect was immediate. Workers stayed on the floor longer. Production numbers climbed back toward their spring and fall levels. Heat related collapses dropped sharply. The fans didn't cool the air. Not really. The temperature inside that Charlotte textile mill was still brutal. But moving air evaporates sweat faster. And evaporating sweat is the body's only real defense against overheating. A fan blowing across your skin in 100° heat can make it feel like 85. That 15° difference was the gap between a worker finishing a shift and a worker being carried out on a stretcher. Word spread fast. By 1915, factories across the Piedmont region of the Carolas through Georgia's textile belt and into the new industrial zones of Birmingham. Alabama had installed banks of electric fans on their factory floors, cotton mills, steel plants, furniture shops, printing operations. If you ran a business that needed human beings to show up and work through a southern summer, you bought fans. It wasn't optional anymore. It was the cost of staying open. And it wasn't just factories. Department stores in downtown Atlanta and Houston figured out something clever. They started advertising the fans themselves as a reason to visit. Signs in storefront windows along Peach Tree Street in Atlanta read, "Cooled by electric fans in big block letters." The Foley Brothers Department Store in Houston put the same promise in their newspaper advertisements. The message was simple. Come inside. It's better in here than out there. Movie theaters took it even further. In the 19s and 1920s, when the film industry was still figuring out how to fill seats during the slowest months of the year, theater owners across the South discovered that electric fans could turn summer from their worst season into their best. The Majestic Theater in Dallas and the Sanger Theater in New Orleans installed massive fan systems that pulled air across blocks of ice and blew the cooled breeze into the auditorium. Audiences packed in during the hottest afternoons, not because the movie was good, but because the theater was the coolest place in the city. This is actually where the idea of the summer blockbuster started. Hollywood released its biggest films in June, July, and August, specifically because that's when Americans were sitting in fan cooled theaters trying to escape the heat. And no, I'm not making that up. The entire concept of the summer movie season traces back to electric fans and ice in southern movie houses. But the most important thing the fan did wasn't economic. It was medical. Before fans reached workingclass neighborhoods, summer in a southern city was genuinely dangerous for the most vulnerable people. Infants and elderly residents in tenement housing and shotgun houses across cities like Memphis, New Orleans, and Savannah died every summer from heat related illness at rates that would shock people today. In some years during the 1890s, infant mortality in New Orleans during the summer months ran as high as 300 deaths per thousand live births in the poorest wards. Three out of every 10 babies born in the hottest neighborhoods didn't survive their first summer. And somehow it gets worse. Those numbers didn't account for still births, which also spiked during heat waves. The introduction of affordable electric fans into these same neighborhoods in the 1910s and 1920s didn't fix everything. Poverty, sanitation, and access to clean water were still enormous problems, but the fans helped. Public health records from cities across the South show measurable drops in summer infant mortality and heat stroke hospitalizations that corresponded almost exactly with the years when fan ownership crossed the threshold into workingclass households. A $5 fan from a Sears catalog couldn't solve systemic poverty, but it could keep a baby alive through an August night in a shotgun house on the outskirts of Jackson, Mississippi. And the fan's reach kept growing. By the mid 1920s, electric fan ownership had penetrated deep into the southern middle class and was making steady inroads into lower inome households. This changed things that are harder to measure than factory output or infant mortality, but just as real. The fan changed what a southern evening felt like. Before fans, summer nights on a porch in Savannah or a backyard in San Antonio were still hot. The air barely moved. You sat outside because indoors was worse. But outside wasn't exactly pleasant either. With a box fan set up on the porch railing or an oscillating floor fan angled through a window, the nighttime ritual transformed. Families could sit together in something resembling comfort. Kids could sleep. Conversations could happen without everyone being too miserable to talk. The hum of the electric fan became the sound of southern summer. that low steady drone coming through screen doors and open windows on every street in every neighborhood in every city below the Mason Dixon line. It was the background noise of porch conversations, of kids chasing fireflies, of grandparents telling stories after dinner. If you grew up anywhere in the American South before the 1960s, the sound of a fan isn't just a sound, it's a whole world. And the population numbers started to reflect all of this. Houston, which had been a small swampy trading post of 16,000 in 1880, grew to 138,000 by 1920. Atlanta more than tripled from 37,000 in 1880 to over 200,000 by 1920. Dallas went from 10,000 to over 150,000 in the same period. Miami, which barely existed as a city before 1900, had grown to almost 30,000 by 1920 and was accelerating fast. These cities were still decades away from the air conditioned sunb belt boom of the 1950s and60s, but the groundwork was being laid right now in the 1910s and 20s by the simple act of putting electric fans in homes, offices, factories, and shops. The fan hadn't conquered the southern heat. Not even close. But it had made the heat manageable. It had turned summers from a season of survival into a season where cities could actually function, where businesses could stay open, where families could live with something approaching normaly. The electric fan didn't build Houston or Atlanta or Dallas, but it kept the door open long enough for those cities to build themselves. If the electric fan had stopped here, this would be a very different story. A story about a quiet little machine that helped a region grow and then settled comfortably into the background of American life. But up to this point, the fan had been winning. It had the whole market, every home, every office, every factory floor that was about to flip. Because in 1902, a 25-year-old engineer at a printing plant in Brooklyn, New York, had been given a completely unrelated problem to solve. His name was Willis Carrier, and he wasn't thinking about comfort or fans or the South at all. He was thinking about humidity and ink. The sack at Wilhelm's lithographing and publishing company in Brooklyn had a problem. Their color printing kept coming out wrong. Pages would wrinkle and stretch during the press run because the humidity inside the plant fluctuated wildly, swelling the paper in ways that threw the ink alignment off by fractions of an inch. For a lithography company doing high-end color work, that was a disaster. Ruined print runs cost money, and the Brooklyn Summers made it worse every year. Willis Carrier was a fresh graduate from Cornell University's engineering program working for the Buffalo Forge Company which manufactured heating and ventilation equipment. Buffalo Forge sent Carrier to the sacket Wilhelm's plant to figure out a way to control the humidity, not the temperature. Nobody asked him to cool anything down. They just wanted the paper to stop warping. Carrier's solution, which he designed in 1902 and installed in 1903, pumped air across chilled coils filled with cold water. As the warm, humid air passed over the coils, the moisture condensed out of it. The air that came out the other side was drier, which solved the paper problem. But it was also cooler, significantly cooler. Carrier had accidentally invented modern air conditioning while trying to fix a printing press. For the next two decades, carriers technology stayed exactly where it started in factories and industrial settings. Textile mills used it to control fiber quality. Tobacco warehouses in the Carolinas used it to regulate the curing process. Pharmaceutical companies used it to keep production environment stable. Air conditioning was an industrial tool, expensive, massive, and completely impractical for homes or small businesses. A carrier system cost thousands of dollars to install and required dedicated mechanical rooms and trained operators to maintain. The electric fan had nothing to worry about. Not yet. The first real crack came in the 1920s when Carrier turned his attention to public spaces. In 1925, the Riverly Theater on Broadway in New York City became one of the first movie theaters in America to install a carrier air conditioning system. The effect on ticket sales was immediate and dramatic. Audiences lined up around the block in the middle of July, not for the film, but for the cold air. Other theaters followed. Department stores followed after that. The Carrier Engineering Corporation began marketing air conditioning as a way to drive foot traffic. And by the late 1920s, cooled air was becoming a competitive advantage in retail and entertainment. But this was still commercial air conditioning. big systems for big buildings. The average American household in 1930 was still relying on the same electric fans that had been doing the job for the previous three decades. A window fan, a desk fan, maybe an oscillating floor model in the living room. Air conditioning was something you experienced at the movies or in a department store downtown. It wasn't something you had at home. That changed after World War II. The post-war economic boom of the late 1940s and 1950s did something that decades of engineering hadn't managed to do. It made air conditioning small enough and cheap enough for regular people. Companies like Carrier, Feders, and Frigid Air began manufacturing compact window-mounted air conditioning units designed for a single room. In 1947, roughly 43,000 window units were sold across the entire United States. By 1953, that number had jumped to over 1 million units per year. By 1955, American factories were producing nearly 2 million window air conditioners annually. The price dropped fast, too. Early window units in the late 1940s cost around $350, roughly equivalent to $3,500 today. By the mid 1950s, competition and manufacturing scale had pushed that down to around $200, and financing plans made them accessible to middleclass families buying new homes in the suburbs. And this is where the story shifts from technology to culture. Because air conditioning didn't just replace the electric fan, it replaced the entire way southerners had been living for generations. The fan had worked with the existing architecture. It complemented open windows, screened porches, high ceilings, and the dog trot breezeways that southern builders had designed for a century. The fan assumed your house was connected to the outside air. It just moved that air around faster. Air conditioning did the opposite. It sealed the house shut, windows closed, porches shrank, and eventually disappeared from new construction entirely. The architectural features that had defined the southern home for over a hundred years. The sleeping porch, the wide piaza, the dog trot breezeway, the transom windows above interior doors, all of it became unnecessary. Builders in the booming suburbs of Houston, Dallas, Atlanta, and Phoenix stopped including them. Why build a sleeping porch when every bedroom has a window unit? Why design for cross vventilation when the house is sealed and cooled mechanically? The porch had been the social center of southern life. It's where neighbors talked, where kids played, where families gathered on summer evenings. When air conditioning moved people inside, the porches emptied. Streets that had buzzed with conversation and activity on summer nights went quiet. People were still there. They were just behind closed doors now, sitting in their cooled living rooms, watching the television sets that had arrived at almost exactly the same time as the window AC units. This wasn't some gradual, gentle shift. Within a single generation, the entire pattern of southern domestic life that had existed for over a century rewired itself around air conditioning. By 1960, over 12% of American homes had air conditioning. By 1970, that number was over 35%. By 1980, it was past 50%. And in the South specifically, the penetration rate was well over 70%. And the consequences went far beyond porches. Air conditioning made the sunbt migration possible. Millions of Americans who would never have considered relocating from the Northeast or Midwest to Houston or Phoenix or Miami suddenly had a reason to go. Affordable housing, lower taxes, growing job markets, and now climate controlled comfort year round. The population of the American South and Southwest exploded through the 1960s,7s, and 80s. Congressional seats followed. Political power shifted. The entire electoral map of the United States was redrawn in part because Willis Carrier fixed a printing press in Brooklyn in 1902, which looking back was either incredibly brave or incredibly stupid, probably both. Everything was in place for the electric fan to disappear completely. The window unit was cheaper every year. Central air conditioning became standard in new construction by the 1970s. The machine that had kept southern cities alive for 40 years was being shoved into closets and garages and attics across the country, replaced by something colder, quieter, and more complete. And the timing of what happened next almost too perfect. Because just as the electric fan seemed finished, just as the last generation that remembered life before air conditioning was getting old, something happened that nobody in the cooling industry expected. The world ran out of cheap energy. In October of 1973, the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries announced an oil embargo against the United States. Within months, energy prices across the country skyrocketed. Gas stations ran dry. Electricity bills doubled and tripled in parts of the South and Southwest, where air conditioning had become so embedded in daily life that people literally couldn't imagine summer without it. Power companies in Texas and Florida begged customers to raise their thermostats. Some cities rolled out brownouts and rolling blackouts to keep the grid from collapsing under the strain of millions of air conditioning units running at full blast. And Americans did something they hadn't done in a generation. They walked into hardware stores and bought electric fans. Sales of box fans, oscillating fans, and ceiling fans surged through the mid 1970s in a way that caught retailers offguard. Ceiling fan sales alone jumped from roughly 200,000 units in 1973 to over 3 12 million units by 1980. The fan hadn't died. It had just been waiting in the attic. The same pattern repeated itself during the energy price spikes of the early 2000s and again during the extreme heat waves and grid failures that started hitting the South and Southwest with increasing frequency in the 2010s and 2020s when the Texas power grid buckled during a massive heat wave. When rolling blackouts swept through parts of the Southeast when electricity bills in Phoenix climbed past $400 a month in summer, the fan came back every single time. Not as a replacement for air conditioning, but as the fallback, the thing that still worked when the grid didn't. And the numbers tell a story that tends to get overlooked. Even in an era of universal air conditioning, the electric fan never stopped selling. The United States alone moves over 100 million fans per year. Globally, the number is closer to 500 million. Ceiling fans, box fans, tower fans, desk fans, industrial fans. They're in bedrooms and kitchens and server rooms and warehouses and hospital wards and classrooms on every continent. The electric fan is one of the most produced appliances in human history, and it has been for over a century. There's something worth sitting with in that fact. Air conditioning is a marvel of engineering. It reshaped the American map, shifted political power, and built the modern sunb belt. Nobody's arguing against that. But air conditioning requires compressors and refrigerants, and enormous amounts of electricity. It needs a functioning power grid, a stable supply chain, and a consumer who can afford the monthly bill. When any one of those things breaks down, air conditioning stops. The fan just needs a plug and a motor. And in the places where those basics are all people have, the fan is still doing the same job it did in a Charlotte textile mill in 1910 or a shotgun house in New Orleans in 1922. It's keeping people alive through the heat. Not in comfort necessarily, not in the sealed climate controlled 72°ree bubble that most Americans now consider normal, but alive, functional, able to sleep, able to work, able to get through another August night. There's a version of American history that gives all the credit to air conditioning. The Sunb Belt story, the population migration, the economic rise of the South, and air conditioning deserves a lot of that credit. But the chapter before air conditioning, the 40 or 50 years when the electric fan was the only thing standing between southern cities and total summer shutdown, that chapter tends to get skipped. It shouldn't be because every skyline you see today in Houston, in Atlanta, in Dallas, in Miami, in Phoenix, those cities didn't start with air conditioning. Air conditioning arrived after the foundation was already laid. The offices were already open. The factories were already running. The families had already moved in. The population had already started to grow. And all of that happened because a machine you can buy today for $15 at any hardware store in America was spinning on a desk, on a factory beam, on a porch railing, keeping the air moving just enough for people to stay. The electric fan didn't conquer the heat. It just held the door open until something bigger came along. And when that bigger thing fails, when the grid goes down and the compressor stops and the house goes silent on the hottest night of the year, the first thing people reach for is the same thing. Skyler Wheeler bolted together in a Manhattan workshop in 1882. A set of blades and a motor still spinning.
fullTextVi: Mùa hè năm 1896, một đợt nắng nóng bao trùm miền đông Hoa Kỳ Kỳ và từ chối rời đi. Trong 10 ngày liên tiếp, nhiệt độ khắp thành phố New York đã vượt quá 100°. Không khí ở khu hạ Manhattan trở nên dày đặc và tĩnh lặng đến mức người dân ở chung cư các tòa nhà ở Lower East Side kéo nệm lên các lối thoát hiểm và mái nhà chỉ để thở. Ngựa kéo ô tô đường phố đổ gục trên con đường lát đá cuội ở Broadway và bị bỏ lại nơi chúng rơi xuống vì thành phố không thể thu gom xác đủ nhanh. Các trung tâm thành phố ở Manhattan và Brooklyn đã hết chỗ trong vòng 72 giờ. Văn phòng điều tra viên thành phố New York đã ghi nhận hơn 1.300 ca tử vong do nắng nóng trong vòng dưới 2 tuần. Và New York thậm chí không phải là nơi tồi tệ nhất. Ở Chicago, công nhân tại các bãi chăn nuôi của Union ở phía nam đã bỏ việc đã đứng. Toàn bộ khu phố ở các khu chung cư trở nên im lặng vì các gia đình không còn đường đi để hạ nhiệt. Không có nước sinh hoạt ở nhiều tòa nhà và không có lối thoát khỏi những căn hộ đã bị lật vào các lò nướng. Bên kia bờ biển phía đông, con số cuối cùng thật đáng kinh ngạc. Hơn 1.500 người chết trong một đợt nắng nóng Điều mà không ai biết vào thời điểm đó là một chiếc máy ồn ào nhỏ đã sẵn sàng trên bàn làm việc ở một số văn phòng giàu có chứa đựng câu trả lời.
